Part 2: Your 15-minute talk

Chapter 13 of 62

Presentation guide: your meeting with the professors

When and how long: Fri 13 Nov, 20 minutes. Test sharing on Teams and Zoom by 22 Nov.

Your 14 slides

The deck you share on Teams or Zoom. Slide 14 is a backup page of references. Open the PDF.

The meeting: online, on Teams or Zoom, on a day the Program sets between 24 November and 2 December 2026 (Japan time). Prof. Zheng will send the details. He told you on 2 November to expect about 10 minutes on your work, 5 minutes on your research proposal, then about 15 minutes of questions. He thinks most questions will be on your proposal, but said they may not be limited to it and depend on which professors join. He expects "Why did you choose Japan?" and "Why did you choose Hiroshima University?".

1. Files in this folder

File What it is
Sudhanshu_Pandit_Hiroshima_presentation.pdf Present this. 14 pages: 13 slides and one backup page of references.
Sudhanshu_Pandit_Hiroshima_presentation.pptx The same deck, editable, with the script in the speaker notes.
FULL_SCRIPT.md What to say, slide by slide: the slide, then the Say lines, then the Next → line that leads into the next slide. The top of the page says how to do the 10- and 5-minute versions.
SLIDE_TEXT.md The words on each slide, and where each fact comes from.
QUESTIONS_ON_THE_SLIDES.md Likely questions on each slide, with short answers.
slides/ One picture per slide, used by FULL_SCRIPT.md.

The deck is built in the deck folder in masters-research. The script lives there as v2/SCRIPT.md, and the speaker notes are made from it. To change a slide or a line: edit build_deck.js or v2/SCRIPT.md, run ./render.sh, then python3 script_tools.py --kit with the path of FULL_SCRIPT.md here. Copy the new PDF, PPTX and render150/slide-N.png pictures (into slides/) here.

2. How to practise

  • Read it aloud. Read FULL_SCRIPT.md out loud twice with the PDF open. Change any sentence that does not sound like you. Keep the facts and numbers the same.
  • Record yourself. Open the PDF in Preview. In QuickTime Player, choose File > New Screen Recording, pick your microphone under Options, and present the whole talk to the screen. Do not stop if you make a mistake. Carry on, as you would in the meeting.
  • Time it from the moment your first slide is on screen:
When you reach You should be at about
Slide 4 (BrandMemory) 2:10
Slide 8 (start of the plan) 5:50
Slide 11 (the model) 8:10
Slide 13 (closing) 10:05
End 10:45

The talk is shorter than 15 minutes on purpose. Do not add words to fill the time.

  • Listen for: speed (calm and clear, about 115 to 120 words a minute, with a pause at each slide change); "like", "right?" and "I would say" (your 2 November review noticed these); each number said clearly ("four hundred twenty-nine", "eight hundred twenty runs"); and the formula on slide 11, said slowly ("p squared, plus the variance of theta").
  • Do three full run-throughs before the meeting, recorded and timed. Do the last one with a friend on Teams or Zoom with real screen sharing. Ask your friend to interrupt you once with a question, and once to say "please skip to your research plan". Then ask them three questions from 05_Questions_on_My_Proposal/.

Do not learn the script word for word. If you know what each slide is for, and the Next → line that takes you to the next one, that is enough.

3. Screen sharing on Teams and on Zoom

Before the meeting day (do this once):

  • As of 12 November, neither Teams nor Zoom is installed in /Applications on this Mac. Install both desktop apps from the official sites. The link you get will decide which one you use, and the desktop apps are more reliable than the browser.
  • Give both apps permission to share your screen: System Settings > Privacy & Security > Screen & System Audio Recording. Turn on Microsoft Teams and Zoom. Quit and reopen each app afterwards. Also check Camera and Microphone in the same place.
  • Do one trial call on each app with a friend. Share the PDF, go through two slides, and ask the friend what they see.
  • PowerPoint and Keynote are not on this Mac. Present the PDF in Preview. It looks the same as the PPTX and needs nothing extra.

Set up the PDF:

  1. Open Sudhanshu_Pandit_Hiroshima_presentation.pdf in Preview.
  2. View > Single Page. Hide the sidebar.
  3. Plan A: share the whole screen with Preview in slideshow (View > Slideshow, or Shift+Command+F). Plan B: share only the Preview window, as a large normal window, not full screen. Try both in your trial call and use the one that looks right on the other side. If window sharing shows a black screen, use Plan A.
  4. Turn on Do Not Disturb (Control Centre > Focus). Quit Slack, Mail, Messages, WhatsApp and Chrome tabs you do not need (see 12_Meeting_Day/01_meeting_day_checklist.md).

On Teams: click Share in the top bar, pick Screen (Plan A) or the Preview window (Plan B), not "PowerPoint Live". A coloured border shows what you are sharing. Ask: "Can you see my slides?" To stop, click Stop sharing at the top.

On Zoom: click the green Share button, pick Screen or the Preview window, then Share. A green border shows what you share. Ask: "Can you see my slides?" To stop, click the red Stop Share at the top.

Moving between slides in Preview: right arrow or Page Down for the next slide, left arrow to go back. In slideshow mode, Esc leaves the slideshow. To jump to a page, leave the slideshow and use Go > Go to Page (Option+Command+G).

Your screen: with one screen, the professors may see anything you put on it while you share. Keep nothing else on the screen. The script lives in your head, and your printed research plan sits on the desk only if they say yes when you ask.

4. If you are cut off, or asked to skip ahead

"Please go to your research plan" or "Please skip ahead":

  • Say "Of course." Press the right arrow until you reach slide 8. From slide 1 that is seven presses. Say the bridge in one line while you go: "In short, every run reads the same rules file, so I want to measure how often runs fail together."
  • Then present slides 8 to 13 as written.

"You have one minute left":

  • Go to slide 12. Say the two expected results in two sentences. Then slide 13: "I can build and run the agents. I want to learn to fit and test reliability models in this lab. Thank you."

A question in the middle of your talk:

  • Answer it briefly. Then: "May I continue with my presentation?" Go on from where you stopped. Do not start the slide again.

The connection drops:

  • Rejoin at once with the same link. If the video is slow, turn your camera off for a moment and keep the audio.
  • When you are back: "Sorry, I lost my connection. Shall I continue from slide ...?" (say the number of the slide you were on).
  • If your internet fails, switch to the phone hotspot (see the meeting day checklist). If you cannot get back in within a few minutes, send the email in 12_Meeting_Day/04_email_templates.md to the address in the meeting email.

Screen sharing fails:

  • Try once more: stop sharing, then share again.
  • If it fails a second time: "Sorry, my screen sharing is not working. May I present without slides? The plan is the same as in my research plan." Then go through the slides from memory, in order, with their Say lines.

They ask you to stop sharing: stop at once and keep talking. They may want to see your face.

5. The shorter versions

The top of FULL_SCRIPT.md has the steps. In short:

  • Full (about 10:45 on the slides): the default. About 5:50 on your work, 4:55 on your plan.
  • 10 minutes (about 9:50): skip slide 3 (Magic Editor), and on slide 7 leave out "The user approves only what they can see."
  • 5 minutes (about 5:15): slide 1 without its first sentence, then "I will go straight to my research plan", seven presses to slide 8, then slides 8 to 13.

If they give you a time you did not plan for, choose the next shorter version. Finishing early is fine. Running over is not.

6. How to point at the formula

Slide 11 has one formula: P(two runs both fail) = p² + Var θ(X), in the black box on the left.

  1. Say where it is first: "In the black box on the left..." The professors may see your slide smaller than you do.
  2. Move the mouse pointer slowly to the formula and hold it still for two or three seconds. In Teams and Zoom, viewers see your pointer when you share. In Preview's slideshow the pointer hides when it does not move, so move it a little to show it. Check this in your trial call.
  3. Read the symbols in words: θ is "theta", ρ is "rho", p² is "p squared", Var is "the variance of", ≈ is "about". So: "Two runs both fail with probability p squared, plus the variance of theta."
  4. Then point at the picture on the right: "In both cases p is 0.2. On the left, both fail 4 percent of the time. On the right, 8 percent."
  5. Practise this one slide five times on its own. It is the slide where a professor will most likely stop you and ask a question.

If they ask you to explain without the slide, say: "If theta is the same for every input, the variance is zero, and two runs fail together with p squared, as if they were independent. If some inputs are harder, the variance is positive, and runs fail together more often."

If they ask about θ(x) and θ(X): small x is one input (the bars in the picture). Capital X is a random input, so Var θ(X) is the variance over all inputs.

7. What is not on the slides, on purpose

  • CV product numbers. The CV says Path AI "handles 1,500+ calls a month at 85%+ accuracy", Magic Editor was "used in 35+ customer workspaces in its first month", and BrandMemory "has built brand profiles for 75+ customer workspaces". They are not in the deck or the script. Here is what your files show. Path AI's 85% comes from your own offline tests, not from live calls: a language model plays a sales lead in multi-turn chats with the agent, and a second model scores each whole conversation (GPT-4o in the first version on 8 December 2025, Claude Sonnet 4 from 10 December, and GPT-4o again from 12 January 2026). The test code is in the Path AI repo, but no saved result showing 85% is on your Mac. The cost saving compares the API cost of the calls with a human sales rep's hourly rate; in your 12 October NU Studio call you said 70%, and the CV says about 75%. For BrandMemory, the 21 October usage check found that, from launch on 10 August, 76 outside workspaces started the website flow, 44 got a finished run and 48 applied a brand identity, so 75+ holds only for workspaces that started it. Nothing on your Mac shows how the 1,500+ calls a month or Magic Editor's 35+ workspaces were measured (the only Magic Editor log covers 14 days up to the 30 September audit: 31 workspaces, with staff not counted separately). For those two, say: "I am not sure how that number was measured, so I will not defend it."
  • Your graduation month. Your CV and the proposal sent on 28 October say May 2026. Your application form and your grade card say July 2026. The deck says only "2026". If asked, say: "My final-semester results were announced on 22 May 2026, and the university's official grade card for that semester is dated 22 July 2026, with a CGPA of 8.04. So May is when the results came out, and July is the date on the grade card, which my application form uses."
  • Yuki for Mac. Its core is a fork of MacOS-Use. If asked about it, say so first. The deck shows only Yuki 2.0, which you started from scratch on 22 September 2026, with no fork and no agent framework. If asked who wrote it, say first that you used coding agents such as Claude Code (most of its commit messages carry a Claude co-author line), then describe your own part in your own words: "The design rules are mine: no screenshots, permission by whether a step can be undone, and a safety checker that sees only the user's words. I checked the agents' changes mostly by measuring what the code does, not by reading every line, for example 45 replayed calls for the safety checker and a blind hold-out set for the secret filter. Without agents it would take me much longer, but I can explain any part of it."
  • The BrandMemory A/B pair. It is no longer in the talk or on the slide. Use it only if they ask what changed after the fix: "After the fix, I compared one pair of demos, with BrandMemory off and on. Contractions went from 6 to 0, and 'you' and 'your' from 15 to 1, as the rules asked. It is one pair, not a study." One output on each side. Never call it a study.
  • The lab's N-version paper. You have read only the abstract. Never quote a number from it, and never say "I read your paper".

8. Likely follow-ups to each slide

For the full set, see QUESTIONS_ON_THE_SLIDES.md: 66 questions on all 14 slides, each with a short answer and three follow-ups.

Short, true answers. The full question bank is in 05_Questions_on_My_Proposal/ and 03_Practice_Meetings/.

  • Slide 2, your paper: "It was a review and concept paper from my first year, with an assistant professor as first author. We had no dataset or model of our own." If they ask what you did: "I did the research and wrote the paper, and my co-authors reviewed it." If they ask what it taught you: "To write it I had to read a lot of papers on brain segmentation, compare their methods fairly and summarise them in my own words. That's where I learned to read a paper properly." If they ask about the award: "The award came from the conference, not from the journal. The paper secured first position at ICRCCT 2023, the International Conference on Recent Trends in Computing and Communication Technologies, on 23 and 24 June 2023, organised by the CSE department of Sri Sairam College of Engineering. The paper itself appeared in IJIRAE, in a June 2023 special issue." Have the certificate ready: it is a Certificate of Appreciation, saved at ~/code/personal/masters-research/2027-refresh/hiroshima-application/_archive/old-prep-folder/01_Your_Documents/ICRCCT_2023_First_Position_Certificate.png. Your CV's line "1st place for Best Research Paper, IJIRAE" does not match it, and the professors may have both. You are fixing the CV line; if they ask, say: "The certificate says first position at ICRCCT 2023. My CV worded it wrongly, and I'm correcting it."
  • Slide 2, Layerpath: if they ask how big it is: "A small team, about 7 people." If they ask whether you're a founder: "No. I joined the founding team as an engineer, and I'm paid a salary only, with no shares or stock options."
  • Slide 4, "What did you fix?": "I removed the per-feature limits of 3,200 characters and raised the overall limit from 6,000 to 30,000 characters. I turned off the default house style when a brand voice is active, and I moved the brand rules before the output requirements." Also true, if they ask what else you found: some rules that did arrive lost to a default house style that used strong words like "MANDATORY".
  • Slide 5, "How big was the test?": "45 replayed calls: 9 actions the user had not asked for, and 36 the user had asked for. It is a small sample, and it is an offline replay, not live use."
  • Slide 6, "What happened with the database?": "The agent hit a problem with the migration tool and ran the change straight on our shared database. The new columns were right, but the migration history still showed the failed attempt, so the next deploy refused to run until we fixed the history." (Source: your memory note ~/.claude/projects/-Users-mafex-code-work/memory/feedback_prisma_migrations.md.)
  • Slide 6, "Do agents follow your rule?": "I have not measured it. That is part of why I want to do this research."
  • Slide 9, "Why not test compliance as an RQ?": "Compliance is only there to show that the change to the file worked. My question is about reliability."
  • Slide 10, "How do you get 820 runs?": "400 main runs: 10 tasks, 2 file versions, Claude Code and Codex, 10 runs each. Then 100 runs for the second Codex model and 200 for my harness at two temperatures, both with the original file only. And 120 runs to screen about 20 tasks, 3 runs per agent."
  • Slide 10, "Why 10 runs?": "Ten lets me see how many runs fail on each input, within budget. The pilot will show whether it is enough."
  • Slide 11, "What if most inputs never fail?": "Then a zero-inflated beta-binomial may fit better. The pilot will show which one fits."
  • Slide 13, "Why this lab?": lead with the lab: "This lab measures how software fails with probability models, and my plan builds on your N-version study." Keep the personal reasons short.
